decks.module: Truck no-zones, passing and wide turns
decks.domain: Sharing the road with motorcycles, trucks, slow vehicles, animals and wildlife

cards.front: How does the handbook say to think of a moving motorcycle, and where are motorcycle laws found?
cards.back: When a motorcycle is in motion, think of it as a person rather than as a machine, and consult the Vermont Motorcycle Manual for motorcycle laws and how to get a motorcycle permit or endorsement.
cards.memory_hook: Think of the rider as a

cards.front: What does the handbook say about how many car and truck crashes happen and who causes them?
cards.back: Each year more than two hundred fifty thousand crashes involve passenger vehicles and large trucks, in more than seventy percent of fatal car and truck crashes the driver of the other vehicle rather than the truck driver caused the crash, and most of these crashes happen in daylight on straight, dry pavement in good weather.

cards.front: What does the handbook say about who is killed in fatal truck crashes?
cards.back: The handbook states that the person killed in four of every five fatal truck crashes is the driver of the other vehicle, and that understanding truck limitations would let motorists avoid many of them.

cards.front: What grows with the size of a truck?
cards.back: The bigger the truck, the bigger the driver's blind spots, the more room it needs to maneuver, the longer it takes to stop, and the longer it takes you to pass it.

cards.front: What are a truck's no-zones, and how can you tell if the driver sees you?
cards.back: Large trucks have blind spots called no-zones around the front, back and sides, a truck could turn into a vehicle hidden there, and if you cannot see the truck's side mirrors the truck driver cannot see you.

cards.front: How should a driver pass a large truck, and when is it safe to return to the lane?
cards.back: Passing a large truck takes longer, so keep a steady speed and make sure you can see the truck's cab in your inside rearview mirror before returning to the right lane, because pulling in front of a truck too soon may force its driver to act quickly to avoid a crash.

cards.front: Why must you never go around a truck that is backing up?
cards.back: A truck driver backing up may have to block the street temporarily to maneuver the trailer, and you must never go around a truck that is preparing to back or is backing, because trailers hide objects and you would enter a blind spot.

cards.front: Why is following a truck closely dangerous?
cards.back: Trucks have long blind spots directly behind them where the driver cannot see you and your own view of traffic is badly reduced, so following too closely greatly raises the chance of a rear end collision with the truck.

cards.front: How do a truck's rear and side blind spots differ in the danger they pose?
cards.back: A truck's rear no-zone hides you from the driver and hides traffic from you, while its side no-zones are where a sudden truck lane change can hit you; the mirror test applies to both.

cards.front: Why are a truck's side blind spots dangerous?
cards.back: Trucks have much larger blind spots on both sides than passenger vehicles, and lingering in them means the truck driver cannot see you, so a sudden lane change by the truck could cause a serious crash.

cards.front: Why must you never cut in between a turning truck and the curb?
cards.back: Truck drivers often swing wide to the left to make a right turn and cannot see vehicles directly behind or beside them, so always watch a truck's turn signals and never cut in between the truck and the curb or shoulder on the right.
cards.memory_hook: Trucks swing wide to turn right

decks.domain: Sharing the road with motorcycles, trucks, slow vehicles, animals and wildlife

cards.front: What rights do motorcyclists have, and what must motorists and riders each avoid?
cards.back: A motorcyclist has the same rights and responsibilities on the highway as any other driver, so motorists must not crowd motorcycles or take the right-of-way from them, while riders in turn must not exploit the cycle's narrow profile and maneuverability.

cards.front: Why should you allow more than four seconds behind a motorcycle?
cards.back: Motorcyclists often slow by downshifting or rolling off the throttle without lighting the brake lamp, so allow more than four seconds of following distance and expect a rider to slow at an intersection without visible warning.

cards.front: Why might a motorcycle's turn signal be misleading?
cards.back: Motorcycle turn signals usually do not cancel themselves, so a rider, especially a beginner, may leave one flashing after a turn or lane change, and a driver should confirm that a motorcycle's signal is real before acting on it.

cards.front: Why do motorcyclists change position within a lane?
cards.back: Motorcyclists shift position within a lane on purpose, to be seen more easily and to reduce the effects of wind, road debris and passing vehicles, not to be reckless or show off.

cards.front: How does a motorcycle's small size distort its apparent speed and distance?
cards.back: A motorcycle's small size makes it appear to travel faster than its true speed and to sit farther away than it really is, so a driver checking traffic before turning at an intersection should assume the motorcycle is closer than it looks.

cards.front: What should a driver assume about a motorcycle's distance and speed at an intersection?
cards.back: A motorcycle looks farther away and faster than it is, so the safe assumption at an intersection is that it is closer and no faster than it appears.
cards.memory_hook: Closer than it looks, not faster

cards.front: Where can a motorcycle be hidden from a driver's view, and what should the driver do?
cards.back: A motorcycle's small size lets it hide behind door posts, mirrors, passengers, bushes, trees, parked cars, fences, bridges and blind spots, so take an extra moment to check traffic thoroughly before changing lanes or turning.

cards.front: How does a motorcycle's stopping distance compare with a car's, and why allow extra space?
cards.back: A motorcycle's stopping distance is nearly the same as a car's, but slippery pavement makes a quick stop hard, so allow extra following distance because a motorcycle cannot always stop on a dime.

cards.front: What limits a motorcycle's ability to dodge, and how does a passenger change things?
cards.back: Maneuverability is a motorcycle strength at slower speeds on good roads, but a driver must not expect the rider to always dodge out of the way, and a passenger makes balance harder, lengthens stopping distance and reduces maneuverability, especially near intersections.

cards.front: Why should you keep at least four seconds behind a motorcycle given its mirrors?
cards.back: Motorcycle mirrors are smaller and usually convex, which shows the rider a smaller image of your vehicle that appears farther back than it is, so keep at least a four second space cushion when following a motorcycle.

cards.front: Why do drivers overlook motorcycles, and what should you watch for at night?
cards.back: Because cars and trucks far outnumber motorcycles some drivers fail to recognize a motorcycle and ignore it unintentionally, so look for motorcycles when checking traffic at intersections, and at night remember that single headlights or taillights blending into traffic may be a motorcycle.

cards.front: How should a driver pass a motorcycle, and what should the driver never do?
cards.back: A motorcycle is entitled to a full lane, so pass it by changing lanes completely, never cut back in too closely after overtaking, use turn signals to tell the rider you intend to pass, change lanes or turn, and never speed up to stay ahead of a motorcycle that is passing you.
cards.memory_hook: A motorcycle gets a full lane

cards.front: How does passing a motorcycle differ from passing a truck?
cards.back: Passing a motorcycle means changing lanes completely because it owns a full lane, whereas passing a truck means waiting until its whole cab shows in your inside mirror before returning.
cards.memory_hook: Passing a motorcycle versus a truck

decks.module: Animals on the road and the penalty
decks.domain: Sharing the road with motorcycles, trucks, slow vehicles, animals and wildlife

cards.front: What rights does a person riding an animal or driving an animal drawn vehicle have, and what must a motorist do?
cards.back: A person riding an animal or driving an animal drawn vehicle on a public highway has all the rights of a motor vehicle driver, and a motorist meeting one must reduce speed and possibly stop to avoid frightening the animal and to protect the rider or driver.
cards.memory_hook: Rights of riders and animal drawn

cards.front: How should a driver behave when meeting, following or passing animals on the road?
cards.back: Never blow the horn or rev the engine, especially on a motorcycle, when meeting, following or passing animals, use the full traffic lane to pass completely without cutting back quickly, and leave at least four seconds behind a ridden horse, a horse and wagon or herded animals.
cards.memory_hook: No horn, full lane, four seconds

cards.front: How does the handbook's advice differ for animals on the road and for aggressive drivers?
cards.back: Around animals the rule is silence and distance, no horn and no revving with four seconds behind, whereas around an aggressive driver the rule is calm avoidance without retaliation.

cards.front: What penalty can follow negligent operation around animals on the highway?
cards.back: A motor vehicle operator may be fined or imprisoned for negligent operation around animals on the highway.

decks.module: Slow moving vehicles and the emblem
decks.domain: Sharing the road with motorcycles, trucks, slow vehicles, animals and wildlife

cards.front: How is a slow moving vehicle identified, and why does early recognition help?
cards.back: A slow moving vehicle such as a tractor or large farm machinery cannot travel at highway speed and carries an orange and red triangular emblem on its rear so motorists recognize it sooner and have more time to slow down.

cards.front: How does the slow moving vehicle emblem differ from a work zone sign?
cards.back: The orange and red triangle on a farm vehicle marks a slow moving vehicle, a different meaning from the orange diamond that marks a work zone.
cards.memory_hook: Farm emblem versus work zone sign

cards.front: What unusual movements can slow moving farm vehicles make?
cards.back: Farm vehicles can swing wide into unmarked field entrances on either side of the road, some equipment is wider than the road, and swaying wagons or implements can hide the operator from view.

cards.front: How should a driver follow a slow moving vehicle, and what rights does its operator have?
cards.back: A slow moving vehicle that delays traffic may pull over when it is possible and safe to let others pass, agricultural operators have a right to use the road, and you should keep a safe following distance, possibly more than four seconds, so that you and the operator can see each other.

cards.front: When may a driver pass a slow moving vehicle?
cards.back: Yield to wide equipment on narrow roads, pass slow moving vehicles cautiously only when conditions are safe and no traffic is oncoming, and stay patient and alert for turning vehicles.

decks.domain: Sharing the road with motorcycles, trucks, slow vehicles, animals and wildlife

cards.front: When and where are moose and deer most likely on the road?
cards.back: A collision with a moose or deer can kill the driver and passengers as well as the animal, so drive cautiously where deer and moose crossing signs are posted, especially in late evening, at night and in early morning when the animals roam and feed.

cards.front: How do deer react to headlights, and why expect a second animal?
cards.back: Headlights may freeze a deer in place or send it bounding at up to forty miles per hour toward its habitat, so a deer on the far side of the road from its habitat may bolt in front of you, and animals travel in pairs so expect a second one after the first.

cards.front: Why is a collision with a moose deadlier than one with a deer?
cards.back: Moose collisions are deadlier because a moose weighs more than a thousand pounds and stands much taller than a deer, so it can land on top of the vehicle with crushing force.

cards.front: Why are moose especially hard to see in the evening?
cards.back: Deer eyes reflect headlights, but a moose stands so tall that its eyes may not reflect and it is more darkly colored than a deer, which makes moose especially hard to see in the evening.

cards.front: Why do deer eyes shine in headlights while a moose's usually do not?
cards.back: Deer eyes shine in headlights but a moose's usually do not because of its height and dark color, which is why moose are the harder animal to spot at dusk.

decks.module: Aggressive drivers and personal wheeled devices
decks.domain: Sharing the road with motorcycles, trucks, slow vehicles, animals and wildlife

cards.front: Why must drivers be especially alert around personal wheeled transportation users?
cards.back: Skateboarders, roller bladers, nonmotorized scooter riders and electric wheelchair users can travel at significant speed, move abruptly and change direction unexpectedly into your path, so drivers must be especially alert and cautious around them.

cards.front: What behaviors mark an aggressive driver, and are they lawful?
cards.back: Aggressive drivers drive too fast, pass unsafely, skip signals for lane changes, weave through traffic, follow too closely and cut off cars, all of which is unlawful and can bring tickets or worse, and they may also yell, honk and flash their lights.

cards.front: How should you respond when an aggressive driver cuts you off?
cards.back: When an aggressive driver cuts you off or acts unsafely, the right response is to keep calm, move out of that driver's way, avoid any challenge and never attempt to get even.
